name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 11 September 1973

clue.text: The goal of the extremist?

blocks.note: surface reading: the political aim a fanatic is fighting for
setter's reading: the extremist goes as far as possible, so the target is the furthest point there is

explanation.surface: A question about what a fanatic is ultimately after.
explanation.walkthrough: The extremist goes to extremes, and the phrase 'go to the LIMIT' names where that ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A limit is the furthest point or boundary, the place someone who pushes everything to extremes is heading for.

clue.text: Formby's street-corner supporters

blocks.note: surface reading: the fans who cheered a performer on the street
setter's reading: George Formby, English comic singer, had a hit with 'Leaning on a Lamp-post' at the corner of the street

explanation.surface: A singer's loyal fans gathered on a street corner.
explanation.walkthrough: George Formby was a British ukulele-playing comedian of the 1930s and 40s; the posts literally hold him up in his song.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamp-posts are the tall street-light posts that stand at corners and that the song's singer leans against.

clue.text: Met to compose choral work

indicators.note: to compose is to put elements together into a new arrangement, as the letters must be

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Musicians gathered to write a piece for a choir.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short sacred choral composition, often unaccompanied.

clue.text: A number of workers in occupation

definitions.note: a phrase for people who are in occupation of a property

blocks.note: ten is a number
worker ants are the classic crossword workers

explanation.surface: A count of people employed in some trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupation' looks like a job; it is the occupying of a house or flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenants are the people who occupy rented property, so they are the ones in occupation.

clue.text: It's very off-putting

blocks.note: surface reading: something thoroughly unpleasant or repellent
setter's reading: literally something that puts people off doing a thing, discouraging an action

explanation.surface: A remark that something is thoroughly unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-putting' usually means disagreeable; here it means what puts would-be offenders off, as a DETERRENT does.
explanation.definitionFit: A deterrent is anything that discourages an action, such as a penalty meant to stop crime.

clue.text: Old party getting at the root of things

definitions.text: getting at the root of things

blocks.note: first meaning: a member of the ..., a 19th-century British reforming political group

blocks.clueFragment: getting at the root of things
blocks.note: second meaning: thorough and fundamental, from Latin radix, root

explanation.surface: A veteran political group trying to tackle underlying causes.
explanation.definitionFit: Radical means going to the fundamentals, from the Latin for root, and also named Britain's old reforming faction.

clue.text: Mission youth delivers the goods

blocks.note: surface reading: a young person from a church mission doing well
setter's reading: a lad whose mission is a small job, carrying parcels to customers

explanation.surface: A boy from a church mission living up to expectations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivers the goods' is an idiom for succeeding, but this youth really delivers goods; an errand is a short mission.
explanation.definitionFit: An errand boy is a lad employed to run short trips, such as taking shopping to customers.

clue.text: Features of those who are long in the tooth' '

definitions.text: Features of those who are long in the tooth

blocks.clueFragment: Features of those who are long in the tooth
blocks.note: surface reading: signs of old age, such as wrinkles
setter's reading: taken literally, animals whose teeth are very long, such as elephants and walruses

explanation.surface: Telltale signs of getting old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long in the tooth' is an idiom for elderly; read literally it describes creatures with elongated teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Tusks are the very long projecting teeth of elephants, walruses and boars.

clue.text: They weren't entitled to the King's Bounty

definitions.text: They weren't entitled to the King's Bounty

blocks.clueFragment: They weren't entitled to the King's Bounty
blocks.note: surface reading: people who had no claim on a royal gift or grant
setter's reading: HMS Bounty, a Royal Navy ship, seized from Captain Bligh in 1789 by members of its own crew

explanation.surface: People turned away from a royal handout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounty' looks like generosity, but it is the ship; those who took her from Bligh had no right to her.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutineers are sailors who rebel against their officers, as Fletcher Christian's men did aboard the Bounty.

clue.text: Makes repairs to a ladder, perhaps

definitions.text: Makes repairs to a ladder, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: fixing the rungs of a set of steps
setter's reading: a ladder is also a run in a stocking, mended with needle and wool

explanation.surface: Someone fixing a broken set of steps.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder in British usage is a run in tights or stockings, which is stitched up rather than nailed.
explanation.definitionFit: To darn is to mend a hole or run in fabric by weaving thread across it.

clue.text: Obvious remedies?

blocks.note: surface reading: cures that anyone could think of
setter's reading: patent can mean obvious, and it also describes branded medicines sold over the counter

explanation.surface: A question about cures so plain anyone would spot them.
explanation.walkthrough: Patent means plain or evident as well as protected by a patent, so the obvious remedies are proprietary ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent medicines are branded proprietary remedies sold without prescription, a phrase whose first word also means evident.

clue.text: Life member of a union

blocks.note: surface reading: someone with permanent membership of a trade union
setter's reading: the union is a marriage, joined for life, with two members

explanation.surface: A long-standing trade unionist with lifetime membership.
explanation.walkthrough: The union is marriage, and each partner is a member of it 'till death us do part'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spouse is a husband or wife, one partner in a marriage.

clue.text: One place your parents can't get you into

definitions.text: One place your parents can't get you into

blocks.clueFragment: One place your parents can't get you into
blocks.note: surface reading: an exclusive club or school that parents lack the influence to enter you for
setter's reading: you are only admitted if you have no living parents

explanation.surface: A grumble about a school or club parents cannot pull strings for.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that only children without parents are admitted.
explanation.definitionFit: An orphanage is a home for children whose mother and father have died.

clue.text: Of course, it's just a summary

definitions.text: Of course, it's just a summary

blocks.clueFragment: Of course, it's just a summary
blocks.note: surface reading: someone dismissing a document as merely a brief outline
setter's reading: not 'naturally' but 'belonging to a course of study', whose outline is being described

explanation.surface: Someone shrugging that a document is only an outline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as 'naturally'; it means a summary of a course of study.
explanation.definitionFit: A syllabus is the outline of topics covered by a course of study.

clue.text: Madly sent gross of birds

indicators.note: acting madly means acting wildly and without order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frantically dispatching a hundred and forty-four birds.
explanation.walkthrough: A gross is twelve dozen, so the surface pictures 144 birds being sent.
explanation.definitionFit: Songsters are songbirds, birds valued for their singing.

clue.text: Mice and men for instance

blocks.note: surface reading: examples of creatures, small and large
setter's reading: Burns wrote that the best-laid schemes of mice and men often go awry

explanation.surface: Mice and humans offered as examples of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns's poem 'To a Mouse' gives the line about the best-laid plans of mice and men, so both are plotters.
explanation.definitionFit: Schemers are people who make plans or plots, as Burns's mice and men do.

clue.text: What comes of growing sage?

blocks.note: surface reading: a gardener's question about what a crop of the herb produces
setter's reading: becoming a sage, a wise person, which brings wisdom

explanation.surface: A gardener asking what comes of planting the herb.
explanation.walkthrough: Sage is the herb in the surface, but here it means wise; growing wise brings wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapience is a formal word for wisdom, the quality a sage has.

clue.text: Exercised right to spread grass below the river

indicators.note: in a down clue, being placed below something means coming after it in the entry

blocks.note: the Exe, the river of Devon, is the crossword's favourite river
R is the abbreviation for right
to ted is to spread mown grass out to dry as hay

explanation.surface: Someone who has worked out by tossing hay about below a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: Ted is an old farming verb for turning and spreading hay to dry.
explanation.definitionFit: To exercise a right or power is to exert it, so exercised and exerted are synonyms.

clue.text: It included Clementine's father's cavern

blocks.note: surface reading: a riddle about where a family lived
setter's reading: the folk song 'Oh My Darling, Clementine' opens by placing her father the miner in a cavern, which its next words set inside a deep gorge

explanation.surface: A riddle about the home of a girl's father.
explanation.walkthrough: In the American folk song, Clementine's father, a forty-niner, dwelt in a cavern inside a CANYON.
explanation.definitionFit: A canyon is a deep gorge, the larger landscape that held the cave named in the song.

clue.text: Shaped like a needle — or a donkey, say?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the made-up word and listen to how it comes out

blocks.note: an ass is a donkey, and -iform means shaped like, so a mock word for donkey-shaped

explanation.surface: Wondering whether something is needle-shaped or donkey-shaped.
explanation.walkthrough: The -iform ending means 'having the form of'; ass-iform is a joke coinage that sounds the same as the real botanical word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aciform, from Latin acus, needle, is a technical term for needle-shaped, as of leaves.

clue.text: Some comedians use them if they are wise

definitions.text: Some comedians use them if they are wise

blocks.clueFragment: Some comedians use them if they are wise
blocks.note: surface reading: sensible comedians make use of certain tools
setter's reading: put 'wise' before the word wanted and you get the quips comedians tell

explanation.surface: Advice that clever comics use certain techniques.
explanation.walkthrough: The ones that are wise are wisecracks, jokes; wise is a prefix, not advice.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracks are jokes or witty remarks, the root of the compound wisecracks.

clue.text: Their act goes with a swing

definitions.text: Their act goes with a swing

blocks.clueFragment: Their act goes with a swing
blocks.note: surface reading: performers whose show is lively and successful
setter's reading: the act is literally performed on a swing high above the circus ring

explanation.surface: Praise for a lively stage act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes with a swing' is an idiom for going well; the performers here really do swing.
explanation.definitionFit: Trapeze artistes are circus acrobats who perform on a bar hung from ropes, which swings.

clue.text: Banned, thanks to obvious disapproval

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks
a boo is a loud, open jeer of disapproval

explanation.surface: Something prohibited because people openly objected.
explanation.definitionFit: Taboo, as an adjective, means prohibited by social custom, forbidden.

clue.text: A reproach that takes on in Somerset

indicators.note: the answer takes a word to become a place, so that place without the word gives the answer

blocks.note: Taunton is the county town of Somerset
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rebuke that catches on among people in Somerset.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is a county in south-west England; its main town, Taunton, is TAUNT with ON added.
explanation.definitionFit: A taunt is a jeering, provoking remark, a form of reproach or insult.

clue.text: Surprising for him to be a little saint

definitions.text: Surprising for him to be a little saint

blocks.clueFragment: Surprising for him to be a little saint
blocks.note: surface reading: a usually naughty boy who has unexpectedly behaved well

blocks.clueFragment: for him to be a little saint
blocks.note: setter's reading: the one named is the opposite of a saint, so such goodness would be a surprise

explanation.surface: A parent amazed that a naughty child has been good.
explanation.walkthrough: A brute or nasty person is the opposite of a saint. Only the A is checked, so this answer is less certain than most.
explanation.definitionFit: A beast, used of a person, is someone cruel or unpleasant, hardly saintly.

clue.text: It's enveloped — with railings perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: something sent inside an envelope along with a letter
second meaning: a fenced-in area, bounded by railings for example

explanation.surface: Something wrapped up and fenced round with railings.
explanation.walkthrough: Railings define the second sense by example: they make a fenced area.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclosure is both a document put in with a letter and an area surrounded by a fence or wall.

clue.text: In the case of 11, they're too much of a good thing

definitions.text: In the case of 11, they're too much of a good thing

blocks.clueFragment: they're too much of a good thing
blocks.note: surface reading: the proverbial excess of something pleasant
setter's reading: with the remedies at 11, too much of them is a dangerous dose

explanation.surface: A warning that you can have too much of a good thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb applies literally to medicines: taking too much is an OVERDOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Overdoses are excessive, harmful quantities of a drug taken at one time.

clue.text: Times change for tiny ones

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its make-up, so the word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that the era is changing for small children.
explanation.definitionFit: Mites are very small creatures or small children, so they are tiny ones.
